<reason>B wins by correctly locking the motion's decision rule: a counterfactual comparison of the same cities today with versus without legal supply, under a modest directional standard. B repeatedly exposed that A's empirical record (Seattle, Denver, Austin, Nashville less affordable than in 2004) measures demand growth against the wrong baseline and never tests the actual counterfactual, while B defused the crash argument with the durable-stock point and the "busts are cyclical, bans are permanent" asymmetry. A was rhetorically superb and landed real hits — Houston/Phoenix as sprawl stories rather than density evidence, B's retreat from its own price-to-income yardstick, and the conceded absence of any realized instance — and these dented B's exemplars. But A's route to victory required supply to have zero or negative net price effect in high-demand cities, a strong claim asserted through confounded trends rather than weighed in magnitudes, and A ran somewhat inconsistent lines (national drivers vs. density as demand magnet). A also spoke last in every round and still left the central comparison standing; a clipped Rebuttal 1 was a minor additional execution cost. B's evidence was hedged, plausible, and citation-free, with cleaner grounding overall.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's counterfactual-baseline reframing (B2.3, B5.1-B5.2) against A's "every permissive metro got less affordable" record: trend-versus-2004 measures demand growth, not supply's effect, and A never compared Seattle-with-cranes to Seattle-that-banned-them — this neutralized A's main route to victory. A's sharpest counter was A4.4, showing B's cheap exemplars were sprawl stories smuggled in as density evidence, which B never answered in the closing.</best_rebuttal>
